201.quote_or_event: “You people are unconscious; you should be afraid of sin.”
201.explanation: In a hymn in Raag Gauree, Guru Tegh Bahadur tells the heedless that what they lack is a healthy dread of wrongdoing.
201.tie_back: The Kural says those steeped in evil feel no fear of it while the truly noble do; Guru Tegh Bahadur likewise treats fearlessness about sin as a sign of being spiritually asleep.
201.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 220, Raag Gauree, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
201._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit on the dread of sin as the mark of an awakened person; the verse does not speak of the noble explicitly or of the swagger that evil brings.

202.quote_or_event: “Virtue and vice do not come by mere words; actions repeated, over and over again, are engraved on the soul. You shall harvest what you plant.”
202.explanation: In Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak teaches that each deed leaves its mark on the soul, so that repeated actions shape a person and bear their own harvest.
202.tie_back: The Kural says evil must be feared more than fire because evil gives rise to further evil; Guru Nanak likewise shows deeds engraving themselves and growing into their own crop.
202.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 4, Japji Sahib, Pauri 20, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
202._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on the self-propagating power of deeds; Japji has no fire comparison, and in Sikh teaching the cycle is finally broken by the Name and divine grace, not by fear alone.

203.quote_or_event: “Fareed, answer evil with goodness; do not fill your mind with anger.”
203.explanation: In a salok preserved in the Guru Granth Sahib, Sheikh Farid tells the seeker to repay those who do evil with good and to keep anger out of the heart.
203.tie_back: The Kural calls refraining from evil even toward those who harm us the highest of all wisdom; Farid gives the same counsel, and goes further by asking for active good in return.
203.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1381, Salok Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
203._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on non-retaliation against those who harm us; Farid frames it as a matter of the heart rather than, as the Kural does, the summit of knowledge.

204.quote_or_event: “Do not harbor evil intentions against others in your mind, and you shall not be troubled, O Siblings of Destiny, O friends.”
204.explanation: In a hymn in Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan forbids even keeping thoughts of harm toward others in the mind, and says that one who does not will be spared trouble himself.
204.tie_back: The Kural forbids plotting another's ruin even absent-mindedly, warning that Virtue will plot the plotter's ruin; Guru Arjan likewise bans evil intent at the level of thought and ties one's own peace to it.
204.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 386, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
204._accuracy_note: Strong fit: both reach down to evil merely held in the mind and link it to one's own suffering; Guru Arjan states the promise positively and has no personified Virtue taking revenge.

205.quote_or_event: “It was not gathered without sin, and it does not go along with the dead.”
205.explanation: In a hymn of Raag Aasaa from the time of Babur's invasion, Guru Nanak says of the riches that ruined their owners that such wealth is never gathered without sin and never goes with anyone at death.
205.tie_back: The Kural forbids doing evil to escape poverty, warning that it only makes one poorer still; Guru Nanak likewise shows wealth won through sin as a loss in the end.
205.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 417, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
205._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the verse condemns sinfully gathered wealth but is about the rich in a time of invasion, not the poor person tempted by need; the Sikh ideal of kirat karni (honest work) is the underlying parallel.

206.quote_or_event: “Fareed, the farmer plants acacia trees, and wishes for grapes. He is spinning wool, but he wishes to wear silk.”
206.explanation: In a salok preserved in the Guru Granth Sahib, Sheikh Farid mocks the person who sows thorny deeds and still expects sweet fruit.
206.tie_back: The Kural says whoever does not wish to be tormented by suffering should never do evil to others; Farid's farmer shows the same folly of wanting a good harvest from a bad sowing.
206.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1379, Salok Sheikh Farid, Salok 23 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
206._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit on reaping what one sows; Farid's image covers all wrong living, not specifically evil done to others.

207.quote_or_event: “Whatever you yourself plant, that is what you shall have to eat; nothing else can be said about this.”
207.explanation: In a hymn in Raag Soohee, Guru Amar Das states that a person must eat the fruit of his own planting, and that there is no arguing with this law.
207.tie_back: The Kural says one may survive any human enmity, but the enmity of one's own evil deeds never dies; Guru Amar Das likewise presents the return of one's deeds as a law from which there is no escape.
207.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 755, Raag Soohee, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
207._accuracy_note: Strong fit on the inescapable return of deeds; the verse lacks the Kural's contrast with outliving human enemies, and Sikh teaching holds that grace can finally free one from this cycle.

208.quote_or_event: “Dadda: Do not blame anyone else; blame instead your own actions. Whatever I did, for that I have suffered; I do not blame anyone else.”
208.explanation: In the acrostic Patti of Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak teaches that suffering comes from one's own actions and that it is wrong to blame others for it.
208.tie_back: The Kural pictures ruin clinging to evildoers like a shadow, something produced by the person himself; Guru Nanak likewise traces a person's suffering back to his own deeds.
208.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 433, Raag Aasaa (Patti), Pauri 21, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
208._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on self-caused suffering; the verse has no shadow image and stresses taking responsibility rather than the constant closeness of ruin.

209.quote_or_event: “Why do you do such evil deeds, that you shall have to suffer so? Do not do any evil at all; look ahead to the future with foresight.”
209.explanation: In a pauri of Asa ki Vaar, the Guru argues from plain self-interest: since one must suffer for one's deeds, one should do no evil at all and look ahead.
209.tie_back: The Kural says that anyone who truly loves himself should not go near evil of any kind, however small; the pauri makes the same appeal to self-interest and demands no evil at all.
209.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 474, Raag Aasaa (Asa ki Vaar, Pauri 21), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
209._accuracy_note: Strong, close fit on avoiding all evil out of care for oneself; the pauris of Asa ki Vaar are traditionally Guru Nanak's, though BaniDB lists this one under a Guru Angad heading because it follows his saloks.

210.quote_or_event: “The path of the faithful shall never be blocked.”
210.explanation: In Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak says that one whose mind accepts and trusts the Name meets no obstacle on life's path.
210.tie_back: The Kural assures that one who never swerves from the straight road into evil is safe from ruin; Guru Nanak likewise promises an unblocked road to those who keep faith.
210.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 3, Japji Sahib, Pauri 14, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
210._accuracy_note: Next-best: both use the image of a path kept safe, but Guru Nanak's assurance rests on faith in the Name, not on avoiding evil deeds as such.
